overview: Freightways is a trans-Tasman express package/courier and information-management group, dual-listed on the NZX (primary) and ASX, with June-30 fiscal year end. It operates two reportable segments: Express Package & Business Mail (multi-brand courier, refrigerated transport and postal networks in New Zealand and, via the 2022 Allied Express and 2025 VT Freight Express acquisitions, Australia) and Information Management (physical document storage/retrieval, secure destruction, medical waste handling and digital records processing across NZ and Australia). FY2025 group revenue was NZ$1,289.6 million, with roughly 82% from Express Package & Business Mail and 18% from Information Management; New Zealand contributed ~64% of external revenue and Australia ~36%, with the Australian share structurally rising as Allied Express and VTFE scale.

business_model.summary: Freightways runs a multi-brand hub-and-spoke courier network (predominantly an independent-contractor delivery fleet) that earns transactional, volume- and weight-based fees per item picked up, processed and delivered, supplemented by a smaller postal/business-mail business. Its Information Management division earns recurring, annuity-like storage fees on physical archive boxes held in owned/leased facilities (very high margin, low churn, billed monthly regardless of retrieval activity) plus project-based/transactional revenue from digitisation, secure destruction and medical/clinical waste handling. Group revenue by product line in FY2025: Express Package & Refrigerated Transport/Storage NZ$994.9m (77%), Destruction Activities NZ$113.4m (9%), Storage & Handling NZ$70.0m (5%), Postal NZ$61.6m (5%), and Other/Digital Services NZ$49.7m (4%).

revenue_streams.name: Information storage & handling (physical archive)
revenue_streams.trend: stable/slowly declining volumes, offset by price

business_model.customer_type: Predominantly B2B - SME and corporate freight/e-commerce shippers, healthcare providers, government and legal/financial services clients for document storage and destruction; contractor courier drivers (not employees) form the delivery workforce under an owner-operator/franchise-like model; no single customer exceeds 10% of external sales revenue
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~64% of FY2025 external revenue (NZ$822.4m), Australia ~36% (NZ$467.2m) and rising - management states 'over a third of our revenue and profits now come from Australia' following the 2022 Allied Express acquisition and the 2025 VT Freight Express (VTFE) bolt-on

main_competitors: Iron Mountain and Recall/Iron Mountain-style records management operators in AU/NZ
competitive_position.market_position: Largest express courier operator in New Zealand via a multi-brand portfolio (New Zealand Couriers, Post Haste, Castle Parcels, NOW Couriers, SUB60 and others) that management positions as #1 or a fast-growing #2 in each niche it competes in; in Australia, Allied Express and VTFE are meaningful but smaller regional/niche players (Allied strong in NSW/VIC oversize and B2C, VTFE strong in Victoria B2B) competing against much larger incumbents (Australia Post/StarTrack, Team Global Express, DHL); Information Management division (TIMG/Shred-X/Med-X) holds a leading position in NZ physical archive storage and a growing but smaller Australian secure-destruction and medical-waste footprint

moat_factors.description: Hub-and-spoke courier networks exhibit strong density/scale economics - shared branch networks, air and road linehaul, and IT infrastructure spread fixed costs across a multi-brand portfolio, making it uneconomic for a new entrant to replicate density without years of volume build

Operating distinct customer-facing brands (premium NZ Couriers vs economy Post Haste vs niche players like SUB60/Kiwi Oversize) on shared back-end infrastructure lets Freightways capture customers across price/service tiers without brand cannibalisation or diluting a single brand's positioning

moat_factors.factor: High switching costs in Information Management storage
moat_factors.description: Physical archive storage customers face meaningful friction (retrieval logistics, compliance risk, cost of migration) to switch providers even as the underlying document volumes structurally shrink, producing highly sticky, contracted, high-margin annuity revenue with 6.5 million boxes in storage across NZ and Australia

Asset-light, variable-cost contractor driver fleet (rather than employed drivers) provides flexibility to scale with volume and shifts some earnings/wage-inflation risk to contractors, though this is the direct target of 2026 NZ employment-law reform (see regulatory risks)

moat_factors.factor: Scale in a fragmented, low-differentiation industry
moat_factors.description: Courier/express delivery is a largely undifferentiated commodity service on any single lane; Freightways' advantage is aggregate national density and multi-brand customer capture rather than a structural technology or patent moat

weaknesses: Express Package is a low-differentiation, price-competitive commodity service with limited pricing power beyond cost-recovery increases; NZ same-customer volumes were flat-to-declining through FY24-25 amid a weak domestic economy

Australian operations (Allied Express, VTFE) are sub-scale relative to national incumbents (Australia Post/StarTrack, Team Global Express) and still building density outside their home states (Allied strongest in NSW/VIC; VTFE strongest in Victoria, assessing NSW expansion)

Information Management's physical storage revenue faces a structurally declining underlying driver (digitisation reduces new paper archive intake over time), requiring continual digital-services diversification (TIMG/Infomedix, Stocka 3PL) to offset the long-run volume decline

Heavy reliance on an independent-contractor driver workforce creates concentrated exposure to New Zealand's 2026 employment-law reform and equivalent Australian 'employee-like worker' gig-economy regulation
TIMG digital revenue can be lumpy/contract-dependent (FY26 H1 saw a 14% decline from the conclusion of a single government project), showing revenue-recognition volatility around large contracts

growth_drivers: Australian express market expansion - both organic (Allied Express 3-year revenue CAGR of 10.8%, EBITA CAGR 16.5%, average 3-year ROI of 15.8%) and inorganic; VT Freight Express (A$71m, completed ~Oct/Nov 2025) adds a complementary B2B niche and management explicitly plans to build share 'organically and through further M&A off the initial density that VTFE provides', including assessing expansion into NSW

E-commerce and cross-border parcel volumes - NZ Express Package item growth increasingly underpinned by cross-border e-commerce work and Freightways Global's international freight/customs-clearance capability, alongside Black Friday/Cyber Monday peak-period volume growth in Australia

Pricing power and margin re-building - Project Evolve (billing/payments infrastructure upgrade, phase two automating pricing/remuneration by weight, size and destination) targeted at recovering c.20-25% wage-cost inflation absorbed since COVID; disciplined price increases executed at the start of FY26 are already driving EBITA margin expansion (13.0% to 13.4% HY25 to HY26)

Temperature-controlled/healthcare logistics - Big Chill (national chilled/frozen FMCG and time-critical transport) and TIMG's healthcare digitisation partnership with Infomedix (Australia's largest private hospital operator, 335,000 patient records digitised in 18 months, expanding footprint from WA/QLD into VIC/NSW) both represent identified 'Horizon 2' growth areas outside the core courier network

Waste renewal/medical waste - Secure Destruction (+5% HY26) and Medical Waste (+8% HY26) are outgrowing the core network, with Shred-X undergoing a network right-sizing and margin-improvement programme in Australia

Infrastructure investment - Christchurch Express Package Hub expansion (South Island network hub, doubling sortation capacity to 70,000 items/night, completion targeted May 2027) and new Big Chill facility (New Plymouth, operational August 2025) support future network capacity and efficiency

business.description: Courier and business-mail volumes are correlated with domestic consumer spending and business activity; FY25 NZ GDP contracted 0.6% and same-customer volumes were soft through FY24-25, though HY26 showed signs of NZ economic improvement and a modest Q2 volume lift

Parcelair JV air-freight partner Airwork was placed in receivership (July 2025); the business continues operating as a going concern under a sale process expected to conclude Q1 2026, and Freightways is separately retiring two 737-400 aircraft for 737-800 replacements in late 2026 (expected cost-neutral, ~$2.4m one-off transition costs) - any disruption to overnight air linehaul would directly affect premium/overnight courier service levels

business.risk: Structural decline of physical document storage
business.description: Underlying paper-archive intake continues to shrink as businesses digitise, requiring the Information Management division to keep growing digital/destruction/medical-waste revenue lines to offset the slow-burn decline in its highest-margin storage annuity

business.risk: Tariff/customs cost changes affecting cross-border e-commerce volume
business.description: A new tariff regime from 1 April (charging $2.21/item for express commercial shipments or $1.28/kg for mail) alters the cost structure for Freightways Global's customs clearance business (~5% of NZ EP volume); it is unclear whether volume migrates from express to mail to avoid higher fees, and Freightways is pursuing mitigation via a postal/UPU clearance channel

financial.risk: Leverage from the Allied Express and VTFE acquisitions
financial.description: Net debt was NZ$587.1m at HY26 (down 6.7% YoY on strong cash generation), and gearing including the VTFE acquisition and lease liabilities is expected to be approximately 55% by FY26 year-end (approximately 35% excluding lease liabilities); management targets the mid-range of its capital management policy by FY26 year-end

The Group reported negative working capital of NZ$45.6 million at FY25 (FY24: NZ$31.2m), driven by contract liabilities (deferred revenue) and current borrowings; management confirms undrawn facilities of NZ$130.9m are sufficient and going concern is not in doubt

financial.risk: Interest rate exposure on bank borrowings
financial.description: Net interest and finance costs were NZ$34.1m in FY25; falling NZ interest rates have been a tailwind (reducing net debt and interest spend, which management explicitly credits for accelerating NPAT growth in HY26), but a reversal would pressure margins given the debt-funded acquisition strategy

regulatory.risk: New Zealand Employment Relations Amendment Act 2026 (contractor 'gateway test')
regulatory.description: Received Royal Assent 20-Feb-2026 and is now in force, introducing a statutory 'gateway test' for contractor classification (written agreement, freedom to work for competitors, control over hours/right to subcontract, ability to decline work without penalty, access to professional advice) following the Supreme Court's November 2025 Rasier Operations (Uber) ruling that gig-economy workers can be employees; Freightways' courier delivery model depends heavily on an independent-contractor driver fleet, so reclassification risk (even if the new gateway test is designed to provide more certainty for genuine contractor arrangements) could materially raise costs (PAYE, holiday pay, KiwiSaver, minimum wage) if contracts do not cleanly satisfy the test

Australia's Fair Work Commission has an evolving 'employee-like worker' regulatory regime for digital-platform and on-demand transport workers; as Allied Express and VTFE scale their Australian contractor fleets, any extension of these protections to freight/courier contracting could increase Australian labour costs and compliance burden

ASX dual-listing triggered Australian Modern Slavery Act reporting obligations across the whole group (not just Australian entities); Freightways is still building out its Supplier Code of Conduct and risk-mitigation programme across 5,000+ suppliers in 30+ countries, an ongoing compliance cost and reputational risk area

macro.description: Truck driver wages rose approximately 20% and NZ minimum wage increases peaked at 25% over a 4-year post-COVID period, structurally eroding margin that management is still working to reclaim through pricing (Pricing for Effort) and Project Evolve automation; cost inflation is described as 'moderate' currently but remains a persistent structural pressure on a labour/contractor-intensive business

A large owned and contracted vehicle/air fleet exposes the group to diesel and jet-fuel price volatility; mitigated only partially by fuel-efficient fleet renewal (Euro 6 trucks, 737-800 aircraft) and surcharge pass-through mechanisms

With over a third of group revenue and profit now from Australia, AUD/NZD movements affect reported NZD results and the foreign currency translation reserve, which has moved from a NZ$9.9m debit to a NZ$12.4m debit over FY2024-25

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ domestic freight/courier volumes are recovering gradually alongside a slowly improving NZ economy (FY25 GDP contracted 0.6%, but HY26 showed 'slight lift' in Q2 volumes); Australian express/parcel demand remains structurally supported by e-commerce growth, though the market is fragmented and dominated by larger national players; physical document storage is a mature, structurally declining but very sticky, high-margin niche being actively managed via digital diversification
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - Express Package & Business Mail volumes correlate with consumer spending, e-commerce activity and business formation/activity in both NZ and Australia; Information Management storage revenue is largely non-cyclical/annuity-like, providing a partial earnings ballast
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - meaningful bank debt (NZ$587m net debt at HY26) funding the Allied Express/VTFE acquisitions means falling NZ interest rates are a direct earnings tailwind (explicitly credited for HY26 NPAT growth acceleration) and rising rates would be a headwind
key_input_costs: Diesel/fuel for owned and contracted vehicle fleet and Parcelair air linehaul
Contractor driver remuneration and NZ/Australian minimum wage settings
Warehouse/depot lease costs (right-of-use assets NZ$325m at FY25)
Customs/tariff costs on cross-border e-commerce (new NZ tariff regime from April)

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results (year ended 30-Jun-2026) scheduled for release before NZX trading opens on Monday 17-Aug-2026, with a same-day investor webinar - not yet released as of this analysis (10-Aug-2026)

HY26 interim results (six months to 31-Dec-2025): revenue +8.5% to NZ$718.2m, EBITA (non-GAAP) +12.2% to NZ$96.5m (margin 13.4%, up from 13.0% HY25), NPAT +17.2% to NZ$52.5m, basic EPS +17.2% to 29.3cps, cash from operations +28.3% to NZ$134.2m, net debt -6.7% to NZ$587.1m, interim dividend +10.5% to 21cps (fully imputed NZ, 46% franked Australia)

Completed acquisition of VT Freight Express (VTFE), an asset-light Victoria-based B2B express operator servicing building, healthcare, retail and plumbing sectors (87 contractors, 49 staff, 350+ clients), for A$71 million; VTFE recorded A$77m revenue in the 12 months to October 2025 and the deal is expected to be ~6% EPS-accretive to Freightways from the first year - a complementary niche to the existing B2C-focused Allied Express

Employment Relations Amendment Act 2026 received Royal Assent (20-Feb) introducing a statutory 'gateway test' for independent contractor classification in New Zealand, following the November 2025 Supreme Court Rasier Operations (Uber) decision - directly relevant given Freightways' contractor-driver delivery model

Airwork, Freightways' JV partner in the Parcelair air-freight network, was placed into receivership; continues operating as a going concern with a sale process expected to conclude around Q1 2026, while both air network suppliers performed as expected through the late-2025 peak season

FY2025 annual results: revenue +6.6% to NZ$1.29bn, EBITA (non-GAAP) +6.3% to NZ$158.4m, NPAT +12.9% to NZ$80.1m, EBITA margin flat at 12.3%, net debt -6.4%, capex/revenue improved to 2.3% (from 2.6%), full-year dividend +8.1% to 40cps; Information Management (IMWR) division EBITA fell 3.1% on weaker Waste Renewal performance, offsetting 6.2% EPBM revenue growth and 11.6% EPBM EBITA growth
Tragic death of a Shred-X (Victoria, Australia) employee; Freightways cooperating with WorkSafe and police investigations and undertaking a review of internal safety systems

Freightways' ASX dual-listing (secondary listing alongside NZX primary) triggered Australian Modern Slavery Act reporting obligations across the whole group, prompting a new group-wide modern slavery risk programme extending to New Zealand operations

Consensus analyst price target approximately NZ$15.3-15.4 (Buy consensus, 5 analysts), against a share price around NZ$14.0-14.2 as of late July/early August 2026, implying modest single-digit analyst-perceived upside; shares have risen roughly 25% over the trailing 12 months

guidance.as_of: HY26 Interim Results (16 February 2026); FY2026 annual results due 17 August 2026 (not yet released)

items.target: Steady improvement expected in H2 FY26
items.notes: Management guided to a gradual continuation of the NZ economic recovery already visible in H1 (Q2 volume uplift in Express and Temperature Controlled transport); no specific numerical volume target given

Driven by Project Evolve automated billing/pricing, Pricing for Effort contractor remuneration reform, and network efficiency initiatives (Shred-X right-sizing, Christchurch hub expansion); no specific numerical margin target disclosed

items.target: Mid-range of Capital Management policy by end of FY26
items.notes: Gearing (including VTFE and lease liabilities) expected at approximately 55% (approximately 35% excluding lease liabilities); management explicitly retains debt headroom for further disciplined bolt-on M&A in Australia
Primary focus is expanding Allied Express or VTFE's geographic footprint or adding an adjacent service, either closely complementary (new state/city) or synergistic bolt-ons

items.vs_prior: raised - HY26 interim dividend 21cps (+10.5% YoY); FY25 full-year dividend 40cps (+8.1% YoY)
items.notes: Dividend imputed at the NZ 28% company tax rate; partially franked in Australia (46% at HY26)

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Mark Troughear characterised HY26 as consistent performance across all businesses with a slight lift in Q2 NZ volumes as economic conditions improve, alongside higher demand for economy over premium courier services (a cost-conscious market). Management explicitly flagged continuing margin re-building as the near-term priority, noted the VTFE acquisition as a deliberate foothold for further organic and inorganic Australian growth, and reiterated a disciplined, complementary M&A approach. No explicit numerical FY26 revenue, EBITA or NPAT guidance ranges were provided in the HY26 presentation; the FY2026 annual result (17-Aug-2026) will be the first checkpoint against this qualitative outlook.

bull_case: Diversified, multi-brand courier network with leading or fast-growing #2 positions in most NZ niches, combined with a genuinely sticky, high-margin Information Management annuity business that partially offsets courier cyclicality

Clear, self-funded margin-recovery story already in evidence - EBITA margin expanded from 13.0% to 13.4% YoY in HY26, NPAT growth (+17.2%) meaningfully outpacing revenue growth (+8.5%), driven by pricing discipline (Pricing for Effort), Project Evolve billing automation and falling interest costs as net debt is paid down

Australian expansion is delivering demonstrated, measurable returns rather than unproven optionality - Allied Express has posted a 10.8% 3-year revenue CAGR, 16.5% 3-year EBITA CAGR and 15.8% average 3-year ROI since the 2022 acquisition, and the 2025 VT Freight Express bolt-on (6% EPS-accretive from year one) extends the playbook into a complementary B2B niche with an explicit further-M&A pipeline

Strong and improving cash generation (HY26 operating cash flow +28.3%) is funding both continued deleveraging (net debt -6.7% YoY) and a progressive, fully-imputed dividend (HY26 interim dividend +10.5%, FY25 full-year dividend +8.1%), appealing to NZX income-oriented investors

Balance sheet retains headroom (targeting mid-range gearing by FY26 year-end) for further disciplined, bolt-on Australian M&A without requiring equity dilution, extending the growth runway beyond the mature NZ courier market
bear_case: Core NZ Express Package business is a low-differentiation, price-competitive commodity service with structurally weak organic growth - NZ EP item growth was just 0.4% in FY25 and same-customer transport volumes fell 5.0%, with the current 'improvement' narrative resting on a gradual and unconfirmed domestic economic recovery rather than a durable structural driver

New Zealand's Employment Relations Amendment Act 2026 introduces a statutory contractor 'gateway test' directly targeting the independent-contractor delivery model Freightways relies on; even if designed to give more certainty, any adverse reclassification exposure (PAYE, holiday pay, minimum wage) could structurally raise the group's largest variable cost line, and Australia's evolving 'employee-like worker' framework poses an analogous risk to Allied Express/VTFE as they scale

Australian operations remain sub-scale against much larger, better-capitalised national incumbents (Australia Post/StarTrack, Team Global Express), meaning continued growth depends on successful integration and further M&A execution rather than organic density that already exists, with real risk of overpaying for future bolt-ons or integration slippage

Information Management's physical storage revenue - the group's highest-margin, most defensible segment - sits on a structurally shrinking underlying volume base (paper archive intake declining as digitisation progresses); the division's FY25 EBITA actually fell 3.1% (Waste Renewal weakness) and HY26 TIMG digital revenue fell 14% on the conclusion of a single government contract, showing the segment's revenue is less smooth/predictable than its 'annuity' framing suggests

Leverage from the Allied Express (A$160m, 2022) and VTFE (A$71m, 2025/26) acquisitions leaves net debt at NZ$587m and gearing (including leases) approaching 55% by FY26 year-end, a level sensitive to any reversal in the currently-favourable falling-interest-rate tailwind that management explicitly credits for accelerating recent profit growth
